blocks.text: Hashing maps a vector to a compact code, usually a short sequence of bits, that can be used to group similar vectors into the same bucket for fast approximate lookup, and locality-sensitive hashing is the specific family of hash functions designed so that nearby vectors are far more likely to land in the same bucket than distant ones, unlike ordinary hashing, which deliberately scatters similar inputs apart.

1. Ordinary Hashing vs Locality-Sensitive Hashing

An ordinary hash function, like the ones used in hash tables and dictionaries, is designed to spread even nearly identical inputs into completely different, unrelated outputs, this avoidance of collisions is exactly the opposite of what is needed for similarity search, where the goal is for similar vectors to collide, landing in the same bucket, far more often than dissimilar ones.

blocks.title: An analogy
blocks.content: Ordinary hashing is like a shredder, deliberately turning similar-looking inputs into unrelated outputs, while locality-sensitive hashing is more like a rough sorting bin, deliberately keeping similar-looking inputs together.

blocks.text: This means the two families are not interchangeable, using an ordinary hash function where a locality-sensitive one is needed will silently break similarity search, since no meaningful bucket structure emerges.
2. What Locality-Sensitive Hashing Guarantees

A locality-sensitive hash family guarantees that the probability two vectors collide, land in the same bucket, is high when the vectors are close together and low when they are far apart, this probabilistic guarantee is what allows an approximate nearest neighbor search to skip comparing against most of the collection and check only the handful of vectors sharing a bucket with the query.

This collision probability can be tuned by adjusting the number of hyperplanes or hash functions used per table, more hyperplanes per code create a stricter, more selective bucket, fewer create a looser, more inclusive one.

This tunability is exactly what lets a single locality-sensitive hashing framework serve very different applications, from near-duplicate detection to approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, just by adjusting the strictness of the bucket criteria.
3. Random Hyperplane Hashing

The random hyperplane method, directly built on the random projection idea from the previous lesson, picks a random direction and assigns a vector one bit, 1 or 0, based on which side of that random hyperplane the vector falls on, using several independent random hyperplanes produces a multi-bit hash code, and vectors that point in similar directions tend to fall on the same side of most hyperplanes, producing matching or nearly matching codes.

code.content:
import numpy as np
def random_hyperplane_hash(vector, hyperplanes):
    projections = vector @ hyperplanes.T
    return (projections > 0).astype(int)   # one bit per hyperplane

hyperplanes = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(8, len(vector)))
code_bits = random_hyperplane_hash(vector, hyperplanes)
print(code_bits)   # e.g. [1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0]

blocks.text: This method is called random projection based hashing precisely because it reuses the exact same random projection machinery covered in the previous lesson, just keeping only the sign of the projection rather than its full numeric value.

blocks.title: Storage tip
blocks.content: A hash code made of 64 bits can be packed into a single 64-bit integer, making bucket lookups and Hamming distance calculations extremely cheap compared to working with the original floating-point vector.

blocks.text: 4. Why Random Hyperplanes Preserve Angle Similarity

The probability that a random hyperplane separates two vectors turns out to be directly proportional to the angle between them, small angle, small chance of separation, large angle, large chance, this elegant relationship is exactly why the fraction of matching bits across many random hyperplanes gives a usable, computable estimate of cosine similarity between the two original vectors.

blocks.title: The core relationship
blocks.content: Probability of a hash bit mismatch equals the angle between the two vectors divided by 180 degrees, so vectors with a small angle between them mismatch on very few of the random hyperplane bits.

code.content:
# empirically checking the angle-mismatch relationship
import numpy as np
angle_deg = 30
theta = np.radians(angle_deg)
print(theta / np.pi)   # theoretical mismatch probability for this angle

blocks.title: Intuition check
blocks.content: Two vectors pointing in nearly the same direction have almost no chance of being separated by a random hyperplane, while two vectors pointing in opposite directions are separated by nearly every random hyperplane.

blocks.text: 5. MinHash for Set Similarity

MinHash is a different locality-sensitive hashing scheme designed for sets rather than continuous vectors, it estimates Jaccard similarity, the size of the intersection of two sets divided by the size of their union, by applying a random permutation to the universe of possible elements and keeping only the minimum element of each set under that permutation, two sets with high overlap are likely to share the same minimum element under a given random permutation.

code.content:
import random
def minhash_signature(set_a, universe, num_hashes=4):
    signature = []
    for i in range(num_hashes):
        random.seed(i)
        perm = universe.copy()
        random.shuffle(perm)
        signature.append(min(perm.index(x) for x in set_a))
    return signature

blocks.text: MinHash is especially useful for deduplicating large text corpora, where each document is represented as a set of overlapping word shingles, and near-duplicate documents, differing by only a sentence or two, still produce highly similar MinHash signatures.
6. SimHash for Document Similarity

SimHash, closely related to the random hyperplane method, is widely used for near-duplicate document detection, each document is first converted to a weighted feature vector, often based on word frequencies, and then hashed down to a compact bit string using random hyperplanes, documents differing by only a small amount of text produce SimHash codes that differ in only a handful of bits, measurable directly with Hamming distance.

blocks.title: Real-world use
blocks.content: SimHash was popularized by large-scale web search engines specifically for detecting near-duplicate web pages among billions of crawled documents, where comparing every pair directly would be computationally impossible.

blocks.text: Because SimHash operates on a weighted feature vector rather than a raw set, it naturally captures how much two documents overlap in emphasis, not just which words are merely present.
7. Hamming Distance Between Hash Codes

Hamming distance counts the number of bit positions at which two equal-length binary codes differ, it is extremely cheap to compute, a bitwise XOR followed by a population count, which is exactly why comparing hash codes with Hamming distance is so much faster than comparing full, original high-dimensional vectors directly.

Modern CPUs provide a dedicated population count instruction that computes Hamming distance between two integers in a single, extremely fast operation, which is part of why bit-packed hash codes are so efficient at query time.
8. Multi-Table Hashing for Better Recall

A single hash table built from a fixed set of random hyperplanes will inevitably miss some true near neighbors that happen to land in a different bucket purely by chance, using several independent hash tables, each with its own separately drawn random hyperplanes, and taking the union of candidates across all tables substantially improves recall at the cost of extra memory and slightly more comparison work.

The number of tables is itself a tunable parameter, more tables raise recall but linearly increase both memory usage, since each table stores its own bucket structure, and query cost, since the query must be hashed and looked up separately in every table.
9. Building a Full LSH Index

A practical LSH index groups vectors by their hash code within each table, using a dictionary keyed by the code tuple, at query time, the query vector is hashed with the same hyperplanes for each table, and every vector sharing a bucket in any table becomes a candidate, the candidates are then ranked by their true distance to the query to produce the final result.

code.content:
from collections import defaultdict
buckets = defaultdict(list)
for idx, vector in enumerate(dataset):
    key = tuple(random_hyperplane_hash(vector, hyperplanes))
    buckets[key].append(idx)

query_key = tuple(random_hyperplane_hash(query, hyperplanes))
candidates = buckets[query_key]

blocks.text: Deleting or updating a vector in this structure just means removing its index from the relevant bucket lists and re-hashing it if its value changed, a much lighter operation than rebalancing a tree-based index.
10. Amplification: AND and OR Constructions

Two standard constructions tune the collision probability curve, an AND construction requires all bits within a table to match, which sharpens the drop-off between similar and dissimilar vectors but risks missing true neighbors, while an OR construction combines several tables so that a match in any single table counts as a candidate, boosting recall at the cost of more candidates to check, real systems typically combine both, several tables, each requiring multiple bits to match.

blocks.text: 11. Choosing the Number of Hash Bits

More hash bits per code create a finer-grained bucketing, reducing false collisions between dissimilar vectors, but also increasing the chance that truly similar vectors are split apart into different buckets purely due to a single unlucky bit, choosing the right number of bits is a balance between bucket precision and recall, usually tuned empirically against a validation set.

A useful rule of thumb is to start with enough bits that the expected number of vectors per bucket is small, a few dozen at most, then adjust based on measured recall against a validation set of known nearest neighbors.

Too many bits per table can also backfire, since it shrinks the average bucket size so much that true neighbors are more easily split apart by a single unlucky hyperplane, matching the same balance discussed for space partitioning depth in the earlier lesson.
12. Hashing vs Tree-Based Search Structures

Tree-based space partitioning structures, covered in the space partitioning lesson earlier in this module, organize the entire collection hierarchically and can adapt well to the actual data distribution, while hash-based methods are simpler, embarrassingly parallel to build, and degrade more gracefully as dimensionality grows, since hash bit assignment does not rely on any recursive splitting of the space.

Hash-based methods also parallelize trivially across machines, since each hash table can be built and queried entirely independently, whereas a single tree structure often requires more careful coordination to shard across multiple machines.

Both families are frequently used together in practice, and the choice ultimately comes down to the specific tradeoffs a system cares about: raw query speed, memory footprint, ease of distributed scaling, or maximum achievable recall.
13. Hashing in Production Vector Databases

While locality-sensitive hashing was historically one of the most popular approximate nearest neighbor techniques, many modern production vector databases now favor graph-based structures for their typically higher recall at a given speed, but hashing remains attractive for extremely large collections where memory efficiency and simple, parallel index construction matter more than squeezing out the last percent of recall.

Some systems use a hybrid design, applying locality-sensitive hashing as a coarse first filter to quickly narrow down billions of vectors to thousands of candidates, then applying a more precise graph-based or exact re-ranking step on just those candidates.

Cloud-scale image and audio search systems have historically relied heavily on locality-sensitive hashing precisely because those domains often have both massive collections and much looser recall requirements than, say, exact document retrieval.
14. A Worked Example
Hash two similar vectors and one dissimilar vector using the same three random hyperplanes and compare the resulting Hamming distances.

code.content:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1)
hyperplanes = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(3, 2))

a = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
b = np.array([1.1, 0.9])     # close to a
d = np.array([-1.0, -1.0])   # far from a

def h(v): return tuple((v @ hyperplanes.T > 0).astype(int))
print(h(a), h(b), h(d))   # a and b likely match closely, d likely differs a lot

blocks.text: Running this same experiment with many different random seeds for the hyperplanes would show that a and b consistently match on most bits, while d consistently mismatches on most bits, confirming the probabilistic guarantee holds on average, even though any single hyperplane draw can occasionally behave unexpectedly.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Using ordinary, collision-avoiding hash functions like MD5 or SHA for similarity search, they scatter similar inputs apart instead of grouping them.
Using too few random hyperplanes, producing hash codes too short to meaningfully distinguish between clusters of vectors.
Relying on a single hash table and being surprised when some true near neighbors are missed, multiple independent tables are usually required for acceptable recall.
Forgetting that locality-sensitive hashing is inherently approximate, some far-apart vectors will occasionally collide and some close vectors will occasionally miss each other.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is expecting locality-sensitive hashing to give exact nearest neighbor results, it is an approximate method by design, always trading some recall for a large speed and memory advantage over exact search.

A sixth common mistake is reusing the same fixed random hyperplanes across unrelated projects or datasets, since the hash quality is tied to the specific relationship between the hyperplanes and the data distribution being searched.
16. Practice: Estimate Cosine Similarity from Hash Bits

Generate 100 random hyperplanes, hash two vectors with a known cosine similarity, and check whether the fraction of matching bits across those 100 hyperplanes roughly approximates the true cosine similarity.

code.content:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(2)
hyperplanes = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(100, 3))
a = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
b = np.array([0.9, 0.436, 0.0])   # small angle from a

code_a = (a @ hyperplanes.T > 0)
code_b = (b @ hyperplanes.T > 0)
match_fraction = (code_a == code_b).mean()
print(match_fraction)   # should be fairly high, since a and b are close in angle

blocks.text: Repeating this same experiment with a much smaller angle between the two vectors should push the match fraction even closer to 1, while a much larger angle should push it closer to 0.5, confirming the relationship between angle and hash bit agreement.
Key Takeaway

Locality-sensitive hashing deliberately inverts the usual goal of hashing, engineering collisions for similar inputs instead of avoiding them, with random hyperplane hashing estimating cosine similarity and MinHash estimating Jaccard similarity, both letting an approximate nearest neighbor search skip the vast majority of the collection by comparing only within a shared bucket.

This lesson builds directly on the random projections lesson just before it, and the multi-table, multi-bit ideas here connect forward to the quantization and product quantization lessons later in this module, which compress vectors in a related but distinct way, by encoding regions of space rather than hashing to buckets.

The AND and OR amplification constructions covered in the newly added section are the standard way production locality-sensitive hashing systems tune the sharp tradeoff between missing true neighbors and returning too many irrelevant candidates.
